title: Lubricate a stiff lock and hinges
intro: Key sticking or hinges squeaking? A dry lube for the lock and a drop of oil sort it.

steps.t: Work out what's wrong: a key that's stiff in the cylinder, a sticking latch or squeaky hinges.
Wipe the key clean with the cloth: any dirt on it ends up in the cylinder every time.
Give one short squirt of dry lubricant (graphite or PTFE) into the keyhole.
Push the key in and out and turn it back and forth about ten times.
Let it dry for a few minutes: the solvent evaporates and leaves a dry film.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Try the key: put it in, turn it and pull it out as usual.
steps.q: Does the key go in and turn easily?
steps.fix: Repeat once. If it's still stiff or the key is worn, get a copy cut from the original or replace the cylinder.

steps.t: With the door open, put a drop of light oil on the latch and push it in and out a few times.
Put 2-3 drops of oil on top of each hinge pin, then open and close the door several times.
Wipe off any oil that runs, on the door and on the floor, straight away.
Open and close the door slowly and listen.
steps.q: Does the door move without squeaking?
steps.fix: If it still squeaks, take the hinge pin out or lift the door off, clean the pin, grease or oil it and refit.

tips: No oil or spray penetrant in the cylinder: they attract dust and gum it up over time.
Frozen outdoor lock? Warm the key, don't force it: if it snaps inside you'll need a locksmith.
Do outside doors once a year: dust and damp are what stiffen cylinders.

title: Draught-proof a window
intro: Cold air around the window? Find the leaks and stick on a seal strip in half an hour.

steps.t: With the window shut, run the back of a damp hand along the edges: where it feels cold, air gets in.
Close the window on a sheet of paper at several points and pull: where it slides out easily, you need a seal.
steps.q: Does the paper slide out easily anywhere?
steps.fix: If it holds everywhere, the draught isn't from the sash: check the shutter box, the sill and the frame-to-wall joint.

steps.t: Pick the thickness: thin strip (E profile) for gaps up to [[3 mm]], thicker (P or D profile) above that.
Measure the sides of the frame where the strip will go and add them up, plus a little extra.
Clean the frame rebate with alcohol and a cloth: no dust, grease or bits of old seal.
Let it dry completely: the adhesive won't stick to a damp surface.
steps.label: Drying

steps.t: Cut the strip to length, one side at a time.
Peel the backing a bit at a time and stick the strip on the frame rebate, where the sash presses when closed.
Press hard with your thumb along the whole strip, corners included.
Close the window and repeat the paper test.
steps.q: Does the window close easily and the paper now grip?
steps.fix: If it's hard to close, the strip is too thick: peel it off and fit a thinner profile.

tips: Work above [[10 °C]]: the adhesive struggles in the cold. Warm the frame with a hairdryer if needed.
PVC or aluminium frames with a worn factory seal: look for the push-in replacement, it lasts longer.
Draught from a roller shutter box? There are insulating panels and brush seals for the strap slot.

title: Replace an interior door handle
intro: Handle loose, broken or just ugly? Fit a new one in about 20 minutes.

steps.t: Look at how the handle is fixed: visible screws on the backplate, or a round rose hiding them.
If there's a tiny grub screw on the handle's neck, undo it with the Allen key.
Prise the rose off with the flat screwdriver in its notch, or undo the backplate screws.
Pull out both handles and the spindle, the square bar that runs through the latch.
Measure the spindle: usually [[8 mm]], sometimes [[7 mm]]. Check the plate type too: keyhole, cylinder or plain.
steps.q: Do the new handle's spindle and plate type match the old ones?
steps.fix: If the spindle differs, use the right one from the box or pick another model. Never force a thicker spindle into the latch.

steps.t: Push the spindle into the latch and fit the first handle, straight and level.
Fit the second handle on the other side and tighten the screws or grub screw fully, keeping the plate straight.
Push the handle down and let go: it should spring back up and the latch should slide in and out.
steps.q: Does the handle spring back and the latch slide freely?
steps.fix: If it stays down, loosen the screws a little: the plate is pinching. If the latch won't move, the spindle isn't seated.

steps.t: Close the door a few times: the latch should catch without you pushing the door.

tips: Take the old spindle to the shop: it's the quickest way to get the right size.
Handle just loose? Tightening the grub screw or the plate screws often fixes it: try before you buy.
If the latch sticks even with no handle on, it's the latch or lock that needs replacing, not the handle.

title: Replace a roller shutter strap
intro: Frayed or snapped strap? Swap it in under an hour without taking the shutter down.

steps.t: Lower the shutter all the way, until it rests on the sill.
Unscrew the cover plate of the strap winder next to the window and pull the winder out of the wall.
Hold the drum, pull out the old strap and let the drum turn slowly until the spring is unwound.
steps.w: The spring is loaded: if the drum slips it spins hard and can pinch your fingers.

steps.t: Climb the ladder and open the shutter box cover above the window: usually screws or clips on the room side.
steps.w: Use a steady stepladder, not a chair: you'll be working with your arms up.

steps.t: Unwind the old strap from the pulley, counting the turns and noting the direction, then unhook it.
Measure the old strap and cut the new one to the same length, plus [[20 cm]] spare.
Hook the new strap onto the pulley and wind it on flat, with the same turns in the same direction.
steps.q: Is the strap wound straight and centred on the pulley?
steps.fix: Unwind it and wind it on flat again: if it overlaps, the shutter jams or the strap wears out quickly.

steps.t: Feed the strap down through the slot to the winder, without twisting it.
Wind up the spring: turn the drum the opposite way to how it unwound, several turns, until it resists.
steps.w: Never let go of a wound drum: it snaps back. Grip it with your whole hand.

steps.t: Holding the drum, slot the strap into it and let it turn slowly until the strap is taut.
Pull the strap: the shutter should rise all the way and the strap should wind back in by itself.
steps.q: Does it go all the way up with the strap pulling back taut?
steps.fix: If it won't reach the top, add turns on the pulley. If the strap stays slack, give the spring a few more turns.

steps.t: Screw the winder back in place and close the shutter box cover.

tips: Measure the width of the old strap before buying: the usual sizes are [[14 mm]], [[22 mm]] and [[23 mm]].
If the spring no longer holds or the box is cracked, replace the whole winder: it's cheap and fits the same hole.
If the shutter is still heavy with a new strap, the problem is in the guide rails or the roller, not the strap.

title: Fix a door that sticks or rubs
intro: Door scraping the frame or floor? Find the spot and fix it, from a screw to a light plane.

steps.t: Close the door slowly and look for where it touches: scuff marks on the edge or on the frame.
Close the door on a sheet of paper and slide it along the edges: where it jams, the door rubs.
steps.q: Have you found where it rubs?
steps.fix: Rub chalk along the door edge, close it, and see where the chalk has transferred or worn off.

steps.t: Open the door and lift the handle: if the door moves up and down, the hinges are loose.
Tighten every hinge screw, on the frame and on the door, until they're firm.
If the hinges have adjustment screws, turn them a little to move the door away from the spot it touches.
Rubbing at the top on the latch side? Swap a short screw in the top hinge, frame side, for a [[70 mm]] one.
Close the door again and repeat the paper test along the whole edge.
steps.q: Does the paper slide freely along the whole edge?
steps.fix: If it still rubs slightly, use sandpaper. If it won't close at all, you'll need to plane: carry on.

steps.t: Still rubbing? Mark the area to take off on the door edge with a pencil.
Take the door off: usually it lifts off the hinge pins; if not, unscrew the hinges from the frame.
steps.w: Doors are heavy and slip: get help and stand it upright against the wall on a cloth.

steps.t: Sand or plane only the marked area, a little at a time: [[1-2 mm]] is usually enough.
Rehang the door, test it, and seal the bare wood with paint or wax so it doesn't soak up moisture.

tips: Only sticks in winter or damp weather? The wood has swollen: tighten the hinges before you plane anything.
Scraping the floor? On lift-off hinges, a washer on the hinge pin often raises it by [[2 mm]].
Fire door, security door or factory-lacquered: don't plane it, call the maker or a joiner.
